title: The Apology of Socrates, Plato
subtitle: 399 BC
subject: litterature
description: In 399 BC, Athens put Socrates on trial. Accused of corrupting the young, he refused to plead for pity. Plato fixed the founding scene of Western philosophy.

hero.hook: A public trial. A man who would rather die than keep quiet.

blocks.text: In **399 BC**, in Athens, **Socrates**, the son of a sculptor and a midwife, went on trial. He was accused of failing to honor the gods of the city and of **corrupting the young**, meaning that he pushed them to question the authorities. The **Apology**, written by his student **Plato**, is not an apology in our sense of the word. In Greek, [[apologia]] means “defense.”

Socrates does not play the repentant defendant. He turns the court into an examination of the city itself. The verdict will be death by **hemlock**, a poisonous plant. The scene will become a founding myth of Western thought.

Athens is coming out of wars and political crises. The defeat by Sparta in 404 still hangs over the city. Socrates questions the powerful in the public square. He exposes people who think they know without ever having checked. Some call that piety. Others call it subversion. The [[sophists]], paid teachers of rhetoric, are part of the same landscape. Socrates sets himself apart from them, but public opinion sometimes lumps them together.

blocks.caption: The trial of Socrates: Athenian democracy judges its own troublemaker

blocks.text: The trial mixes religion and politics. What stands accused is not only a set of abstract ideas. It is a way of life that unsettles people: a man who spends his days asking questions, holding no official post, and never falling silent in front of the powerful.

Socrates tells the story of the **oracle of Delphi**, the sanctuary where the priestess of **Apollo** delivered answers from the gods. The oracle said that no one was wiser than he was. He concluded that his wisdom was **negative**. Other men believe they know. He knows that he does not. Hence the famous line: [[“I know that I know nothing”]].
His method, [[Socratic maieutics]], compares dialogue to a birth: drawing a clearer thought out of the other person through one question after another, without imposing a ready-made lesson.
In court, that stance grates. Instead of begging, Socrates explains why an **unexamined life** is not worth defending. He would rather die than betray his mission.

Found guilty, Socrates has to propose an alternative to the death penalty. Instead of a prudent exile, he suggests being fed at the [[Prytaneum]], the public building in Athens where the city honored its benefactors. The provocation is calculated. The jurors vote for death.

blocks.caption: The Death of Socrates by David: the philosopher's calm in front of the hemlock

blocks.text: Later, in the dialogue **Crito**, another text by Plato, he refuses to escape. Obeying the laws in form while criticizing them in substance: the Socratic paradox starts here. Socrates accepts the sentence in order to stay consistent with his whole life.

sections.title: The birth of a philosophical myth

blocks.text: Plato makes this death the baptism of philosophy. Thinking can cost you dearly. The Apology inspired the Stoics, the Christians, the **Enlightenment** of the 18th century, and modern resisters. It fixed one image: the wise man who prefers truth to comfortable survival.

This account is not a neutral transcript. Plato chooses what should be remembered: a stance, not only a set of arguments. After Socrates, doing philosophy also means accepting that the truth can be expensive in public life. The Apology remains the first great text in which thought defends itself against power.
The **Apology of Socrates** shows a man who refuses to beg for his life. In **399**, Athens killed an inconvenient citizen and invented, in spite of itself, the martyr of free thought.
